section.title: Chapter review and applications
section.p: This chapter began with a simple change in perspective. Instead of being handed a function and asked to differentiate it, we were asked to build the function first.

A ladder slides. A box is folded. A cup cools. A population grows. A light ray chooses a path. In each case, the derivative did not appear at the beginning. It appeared after we translated the situation into mathematics.
That is the main skill of the chapter:
The last step is as important as the first. A derivative answer without units, sign, domain, and meaning is not yet an answer to the problem.

subsection.title: The chapter in one map
subsection.p: The chapter used derivatives in several different ways. The same derivative idea kept returning with different names.

md.mrow: \text{optimization} \amp \text{Which choice is best?} \amp \text{find and test candidates}
\text{linear approximation} \amp \text{How much does the output change?} \amp \Delta y\approx f'(x)\Delta x
\text{Newton's method} \amp \text{Where is a zero?} \amp \text{use tangent-line correction}
\text{exponential models} \amp \text{What grows at a rate proportional to itself?} \amp y'=ky
\text{logistic models} \amp \text{How does growth slow near a limit?} \amp P'=rP\left(1-\dfrac{P}{K}\right)

figure.caption: The chapter’s methods all follow the same modeling path: translate, differentiate, solve, and interpret.

note.title: A derivative answer must still pass three checks
note.md: \text{Is the answer allowed by the domain of the model?}

subsection.p: These checks are not afterthoughts. They are part of the mathematics.

exercise.title: Why is the main skill of the chapter building the function first?

statement.p: A ladder slides, a box is folded, a cup cools, a population grows. In your own words, why did the derivative appear after we translated the situation into mathematics, and why is that change of perspective the chapter’s central idea?

hint.p: Real situation, then model, then derivative information, then interpretation. We were not handed a function and asked to differentiate it.

subsection.title: Skills: related rates and optimization
subsection.p: Related rates and optimization are the two main problem-solving skills of this chapter. They look similar because both begin with translation, but they ask different questions.

md.mrow: \begin{array}{c|c|c} problem type \amp what changes? \amp what is the goal?
\hline \text{related rates} \amp \text{quantities change with time} \amp \text{find an unknown rate}
\text{optimization} \amp \text{a choice variable changes} \amp \text{maximize or minimize a quantity} \end{array}

paragraphs.title: Related rates checklist

md.mrow: \begin{array}{ll} \text{1.} \amp \text{Draw a picture, if geometry is involved.}
\text{2.} \amp \text{Name the changing quantities as functions of time.}
\text{5.} \amp \text{Substitute values for the instant in question.}

paragraphs.p: The most common mistake is substituting the instant-specific numbers too early. The variables must remain variables until after the relation has been differentiated.

paragraphs.title: Optimization checklist

md.mrow: \text{5.} \amp \text{Use the constraint to get one variable.}
\text{8.} \amp \text{Translate the result back into the situation.} \end{array}

paragraphs.p: The most common mistake is finding a critical point and stopping. A critical point is a candidate, not a conclusion.

exercise.title: Why do related rates, optimization, and models use the same derivative differently?

statement.p: Related rates differentiate a relation. Optimization finds and tests candidates. Exponential and logistic models begin with a law for y'. In your own words, why is the derivative doing one job with several names, and how do you tell which question a problem is asking?

hint.p: Ask whether the problem wants a rate, a best choice, a small-error estimate, a root, or a function obeying a rate law.

note.title: What the project tests
note.p: A model is not only a formula that fits numbers. It should also respect the behavior of the situation. A cooling object should approach room temperature, not pass below it because a line keeps decreasing forever.

exercise.title: Why is a model a promise with conditions?

statement.p: Exponential growth promises a constant relative rate. Logistic growth adds a fixed carrying capacity. In your own words, why must we check whether that promise matches the situation before trusting a formula, and what goes wrong if the conditions are invisible in the early data?

hint.p: A formula can be mathematically correct and still be the wrong story. Early exponential-looking data may hide a later ceiling.

statement.p: Sign, units, and domain are listed as part of the mathematics, not as afterthoughts. In your own words, why can a correctly computed derivative still fail to answer the original problem if one of those checks is skipped?

hint.p: A number without direction, units, or feasibility is not yet an answer to a related-rates, optimization, or modeling question.

subsection.title: Where this points
subsection.p: This chapter showed how much can be done with a derivative.
A derivative can relate changing quantities. It can find a best choice. It can estimate error. It can turn a tangent line into a root-finding method. It can express a physical law such as
or
But a derivative is still local. It tells how fast something is changing at an instant.
Many questions ask for the accumulated result of those changes.
If velocity is known at every instant, how far did the object travel?
If a force changes with position, how much work was done?
If density varies along a rod, what is the rod’s total mass?
If a rate law tells how a quantity changes, how much total change has occurred over an interval?
Those questions return us to the dashboard from the beginning of the book. The speedometer gives rate. The odometer gives accumulation.
The next chapter builds the second great operation of calculus: adding up infinitely many small changes.
